newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik tanks move into rebel colonel's town.
newsitem.headline: Tajik tanks move into rebel colonel's town.

text.p: Government tanks on Friday entered the southern Tajikistan town of Kurgan Tyube, stronghold of rebel Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev, residents said.
Contacted by telephone, they said Khudoyberdyev, his family and guards had fled his house in the town and moved into the barracks of his elite brigade on its outskirts.
Armed looters went through his house after he vacated it. The residents heard no fighting but said they saw at least three government tanks near the town's only bus station.
Zafar Saidov, spokesman for President Imomali Rakhmonov, told Reuters the colonel's forces left their base at 1400 GMT and headed southwest. There was no independent confirmation of this.
Saidov said Khudoyberdyev might try to cross into Afghanistan or Uzbekistan.
The politically ambitious Khudoyberdyev moved his armour towards Dushanbe, 110 km (70 miles) to the north, last weekend after fighting between two rival warlords in the capital.
He appeared to suffer some defeats in four days of fighting and Rakhmonov said on Wednesday the colonel had been dismissed.
Khodoyberdyev refused to obey the order and said on Thursday he was ready to resume fighting because the government had failed to withdraw its troops from around Kurgan Tyube, as agreed on Wednesday.
"Honestly, I think it could only be war," he said in an interview in Kurgan Tyube.

Russia's Interfax news agency quoted the rebel brigade's chief of staff, Ergash Khasanov, as saying "our corps will not hand over its weapons" because heavy artillery and pro-government forces had not withdrawn.

Itar-Tass news agency said talks between Khudoyberdyev and a senior commander from Russian-led peacekeeping forces had failed. The talks near Khudoyberdyev's headquarters in Kurgan Tyube lasted just five minutes, it said.
Moscow has played a low-key role but is concerned about stability in Tajikistan, which borders Afghanistan and is seen by Russia as a buffer against any spread of Islamic fundamentalism.
Khudoyberdyev's house in Kurgan Tyube came under attack on Thursday from what the rebel leader said were government troops.
Fighting erupted in Dushanbe only weeks after Rakhmonov signed a peace agreement with Islamic opposition guerrillas aimed at ending four years of civil war in Tajikistan.
The guerrillas were not involved in the latest clashes, but Khudoyberdyev joined the fray, moving his brigade towards the capital last Saturday.
Rakhmonov blamed the unrest on a "third force" opposed to his peace deal with the Islamists and mafia groups operating in the republic.
"Active agitation, led by a 'third force' against the Tajik peace accord, has helped to bring about this mood of revenge," Rakhmonov told the Russian daily Izvestia.
Khudoyberdyev opposes the return of armed Islamist guerrillas to Dushanbe, agreed under the peace deal.
He used the issue to declare autonomy for his Kurgan Tyube southwestern region last month, setting up a "Defence Council" to run it in a move deemed "unconstitutional" by Dushanbe.
Western observers say also that rival warlords -- all nominally loyal to Rakhmonov -- are battling for turf in the republic, its economy shattered by the civil war.
